# ADR 049 — Cross-project edges stay untyped; SHACL validates the union of project graphs — consolidated view

## 0. Decision

A project's named graph is **subject-complete and object-open**: it holds
every projected triple whose subject the project owns — its Project node and
its tasks — and no triple about any other subject. A cross-project edge's
foreign endpoint therefore appears in that graph as a bare object IRI with no
`rdf:type` beside it, **by design**. The projector never emits a type stub
and never mirrors a foreign task.

Correspondingly, SHACL validation of projected data is defined over the
**union of the project named graphs** (their RDF merge, plus the TBox — the
ontology's class and property definitions), never over a single project
graph. A foreign endpoint's `rdf:type` is found in its
home graph, where it is authoritative; `sh:class` constraints hold across the
union. No per-graph validation gate is ever introduced.

The projector as shipped (WL-26) already produces exactly this shape —
`TestCrossProjectEdgeProjectsBothGraphs` (`internal/projector/projector_test.go`)
pins it — so this ADR ratifies existing output and constrains the future
validation gate. No code changes.

## 1. The problem

The projector renders one named graph per project and replaces it whole via
a Graph Store Protocol (GSP) `PUT` (006 §11). A `blocks`/`child_of`/`follow_up_to` edge that crosses
projects lands `A wl:blocks B` in P1's graph and `B wl:dependsOn A` in P2's;
neither graph holds both ends, so each carries an object IRI it says nothing
else about. Nothing validates projected data today — the 006 §7 SHACL tier
gates authored vocabulary fixtures in CI, and no gate over graph-server
content exists — but the moment one validates a project graph in isolation,
`wl:followUpTo`'s `sh:class wl:Task` (`ns/shapes.ttl`) fails on the foreign,
locally-untyped end. WL-26 deliberately shipped without deciding how the
foreign end gets its type; this ADR owns that decision.

## 2. What a project graph promises

The named graph is the projector's **write and replace unit**, chosen so that
re-rendering a dirty project is idempotent (006 §11) — it was never a
semantic completeness boundary. This ADR makes the boundary explicit:

- **Subject-complete**: the graph carries every projected triple whose
  subject is the project's Project node or one of its tasks.
  `graphproj.TaskTriples` already enforces this per task (every triple it
  returns has the task as subject); the property now holds for the graph as a
  whole.
- **Object-open**: an object IRI is a global name, not a local row. Its
  description — type included — lives in the graph of the project that owns
  it. This is ordinary linked-data practice, and it is already how the
  runtime tier reads: Oxigraph queries run over the dataset (`GRAPH` patterns
  and the union default graph), so `?t wl:dependsOn+ ?x` reachability never
  needed the foreign end typed locally either.

A consumer that fetches one project graph gets a self-consistent description
of that project's own work, with resolvable IRIs at the edges. It does not
get a closed world — a self-contained, complete picture — and must not
validate the graph in isolation (§3).

## 3. Validation scope

When a SHACL gate over projected data lands, its data graph is the union of
every project named graph on the work branch, plus `ns/ontology.ttl` for
`rdfs:subClassOf` resolution. This makes validation a batch operation — a CI
job or a periodic sweep reading graph-server — never a per-`PUT` gate.

Per-`PUT` validation would be flaky by construction, not just mis-scoped: one
edge write logs both endpoint tasks (`AddEdge` in `internal/store/tasks.go`
calls `LogChange` for each end), so both projects go dirty and both graphs
re-render — but sequentially, and at worst in adjacent batches when the two
log rows straddle `DirtyProjects`' batch limit. Between the two `PUT`s the
union is momentarily asymmetric. A union validator therefore runs against a
drained projector (checkpoint caught up), or tolerates and retries; either
way every steady state validates.

A dangling endpoint that is *not* transient — an edge whose far end never
appears in any graph — surfaces under union validation as the `sh:class`
violation it deserves to be. That is the referential-integrity check working,
and it is exactly the signal a locally-asserted stub would have destroyed.

## 4. Consequences

**The projector is finished as shipped.** No stub emission, no mirroring, no
cross-project dirtiness propagation. The decision is recorded here and in the
006 amendments; the code already conforms.

**No single project graph self-validates, and none ever will.** A future
consumer wanting "fetch one graph, validate it" is asking for a property this
ADR deliberately declines to promise, because buying it costs either
duplicated facts or weakened shapes (§5). Such a consumer validates the union
or trusts the producer.

**`sh:class` keeps its teeth.** The constraint checks the type asserted by
the endpoint's owning projection. A projector-emitted stub would assert the
very fact the constraint exists to verify, making a mistyped or nonexistent
endpoint validate vacuously.

**Validation inherits eventual consistency.** The gate is a sweep over a
converged store, not an admission control on writes. That matches the
projector's own contract (idempotent re-render, self-healing checkpoint) and
costs nothing a per-graph gate would have saved.

## 5. Rejected alternatives

- **Emit a bare `rdf:type wl:Task` stub for foreign endpoints.**
  Self-defeating: `wl:TaskShape` targets `sh:targetClass wl:Task` and
  requires ≥1 `wl:taskKind`, exactly one `wl:taskState`, exactly one
  `wl:priority`, exactly one `wl:inProject` — a bare stub becomes a shape
  target and fails four constraints, so per-graph validation still fails,
  just differently. It also asserts the fact validation is meant to check
  (§4). Rejected.
- **Mirror the foreign task in full.** Passes the shape but forks authority —
  one subject described authoritatively in two graphs, against the one-owner
  rule the backbone/graph split is built on — and goes stale: a state change
  in P2 dirties only P2, so P1's copy of the foreign task is wrong until
  unrelated P1 activity happens to re-render it. Fixing the staleness means
  propagating dirtiness across the edge graph, with write amplification
  proportional to cross-project coupling. Rejected.
- **Weaken `wl:TaskShape`'s targeting so stubs escape** (e.g.
  `sh:targetSubjectsOf wl:inProject` instead of `sh:targetClass`). Encodes
  "stub-ness" as an absence, and exempts a genuinely malformed resident task
  that lost its `wl:inProject` — the defect the shape's `minCount` exists to
  catch. Rejected.
